quiz.p: Which is the best reason that many birds migrate?
opts: The food they need is in different places at different times of the year
They get bored of one place
Every bird is hurt by cold
quiz.why: Migration follows food, space and safety for raising young. Cold is only one reason food runs short. Crows and sparrows stay through cold winters because they can still find food.

quiz.p: Why do so many birds travel to the far north to raise chicks in summer?
opts: The days are very long, so they have many hours to feed and food is plentiful
The far north is warmer than India in summer
There are no other birds there
quiz.why: The tilt of the Earth gives the far north very long summer days. Plants, insects and mudflat animals thrive in that light. A bird can feed her chicks for many hours a day.

quiz.p: How different is the length of the day in Kerala in June and in December?
opts: Only a little different, about the same length
Twice as long in June
There is no daylight in December
quiz.why: Near the equator, day length changes only a little all year, a few minutes each week at most. The big changes are far north and far south.

quiz.p: Why do migrating birds store fat rather than sugar as fuel?
opts: A gram of fat holds more than twice the energy of a gram of sugar, so she carries less weight
Fat is lighter than sugar
Sugar cannot be stored
quiz.why: A flying bird must carry her own fuel, so fuel that holds more energy per gram lets her fly farther on the same load. Fat holds about 9 units of energy per gram and sugar about 4.

quiz.p: What happens to a godwit's gut before a very long flight?
opts: It shrinks, and the flight muscles grow
It grows bigger to hold food
Nothing changes
quiz.why: A gut full of food is heavy, and she will not eat on the flight. The body saves weight by making the gut smaller and builds more muscle for flying. After landing, the gut grows back.

opts: A place on a journey where a bird rests and feeds before flying on
A place where a bird stays all year
The end of a bird's journey
quiz.why: A stopover is a refuelling place. The bird feeds there for days or weeks to build up fat for the next stage.

quiz.p: A key lake on a flyway is drained. What is the most likely result?
opts: Fewer birds arrive at the next place, because some run out of fuel in the gap
Nothing changes, because birds can fly forever
More birds arrive, because the route is shorter
quiz.why: A drained lake makes a longer gap between refuelling places. A bird carries a limited amount of fuel, so more of them fall short. Our dice model showed that.

quiz.p: A small falcon is in a town for three weeks in October, then moves on to Africa. Which label do birders give her?
opts: Passage migrant
Resident
Winter visitor
quiz.why: A passage migrant stops only for days or weeks on the way somewhere else. A winter visitor stays for the whole northern winter. A resident stays all year.

quiz.p: On a tracking graph of a bird's position, the line stays flat for four weeks. What does it show?
opts: The bird stayed in about the same place for four weeks
The bird flew four weeks without stopping
The tag was broken
quiz.why: A flat line means the position is not changing, so the bird is resting or feeding in one place. A steep line shows a flight.

quiz.p: Why must a satellite tag weigh very little?
opts: A heavy tag makes flying costly and may change how the bird behaves
A heavy tag is easier to lose
A light tag gives better pictures
quiz.why: A tag is extra weight that the bird carries on every wingbeat. A common rule is that it should be only a few parts in a hundred of her weight.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not fully understand?
opts: How a young bird, who has never made the trip, times her journey and finds the way
Whether birds travel from one country to another
Whether birds store fat
quiz.why: We know that day length and an inside yearly clock both play a part, but how they work together is still being studied. Rings and tags have shown that the journeys are real.
False. Olive ridley turtles, hilsa fish, butterflies, elephants and many other animals make regular seasonal journeys. Some, such as the wallcreeper, move only up and down a mountain.

worksheets.title: Migration: how a body is built for a journey (core)

items.p: What does the word migration mean?
opts: A regular journey that an animal makes each year, going out and coming back
Flying very high
Moving house once in a lifetime
items.why: Migration is a regular, seasonal journey. The animal goes out and comes back, year after year.

items.p: A bird that comes to India only for the northern winter and then leaves is called a ____ visitor.
items.why: A winter visitor comes for the cold months of the north and goes back to breed. A summer visitor does the opposite.

items.p: Birds migrate only because winter is cold.
items.why: False. The main reason is food. Some birds stay through freezing winters, and some migrate from warm places. Cold matters only because it makes food scarce.

items.p: Sort each bird by her year in a city in India.
items.why: Sparrows, peafowl and crows live here all year. Bar-headed geese, common sandpipers and shovelers are winter visitors that breed far to the north.

items.p: Which holds more energy in each gram?
opts: Fat
Sugar
They hold the same
items.why: A gram of fat holds more than twice as much energy as a gram of sugar. That is why a bird that must carry her fuel stores fat.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for how a wader gets ready for a long flight.
a: The days are long and food is plentiful
The bird eats much more than usual
She stores the extra energy as fat
Her gut shrinks and her flight muscles grow
She flies and burns the fat
items.why: Food comes first. Then she eats extra, stores it as fat, and rebuilds her body before the flight. In the air, she burns the fat.

items.p: Explain in two sentences why a godwit's gut gets smaller before a long flight.
items.a: A big gut full of food is heavy, and she will not eat during the flight. A smaller gut saves weight, and bigger flight muscles give more power.
items.why: A strong answer says that the gut is heavy and not needed in the air, and links that to saving weight or making room for muscles.

items.p: Match each place in India to what it is for animals.
pairs: a wintering ground and stopover for water birds
a wetland where Siberian cranes once wintered
beaches where olive ridley turtles come to nest
a place where Amur falcons gather in autumn
items.why: Chilika holds many wintering water birds. Keoladeo once hosted the Siberian crane. Gahirmatha and Rushikulya have the mass nesting of turtles. Amur falcons roost around the Doyang reservoir.

items.p: Which tool tells you the most about a bird's whole route, week by week?
opts: A satellite tag
A ring on her leg
A photo of her at a lake
items.why: A ring tells you two points on the journey, where she was ringed and where she was found. A satellite tag sends her position for months, so you can see the whole route.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a godwit before a long flight, cut open. Label the three parts: fat, flight muscle and gut.
items.art: A cut-away drawing of a godwit with a thick layer of fat under the skin, large chest muscles and a small gut.
a: Thick layer under the skin: fat
Large muscle in the chest: flight muscle
items.why: Before a long flight the fat layer is thick, the chest muscles are large, and the gut is small.

items.p: A tag on a bird can weigh as much as the scientists like.
items.why: False. A tag adds weight that the bird must carry on every wingbeat. Scientists keep it to a few parts in a hundred of her weight.

items.p: A godwit weighs 400 grams without fat. Before leaving she adds 300 grams of fat. How many grams does she weigh at take-off?
items.why: 400 plus 300 is 700. So 300 of her 700 grams is fat, a little less than half.

items.p: A village wants a road along the shore of a lake that is a stopover for thousands of waders.

views.who: Meera, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The lake should be left alone. If the waders cannot feed there, they may not reach the next place.

views.who: Arif, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The village needs the road to reach the hospital and the school. A plan can protect both.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you suggest?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side or a middle path, gives a reason, and uses what we know: waders need shallow mud, and people need a road.
items.why: Both views have a point. The best answers think about a plan that gives the birds quiet mud and the village its road.

items.p: Draw a graph line for a bird that rests at a lake for 3 weeks, flies south for 1 week, then rests at another lake for 3 weeks.
items.a: A line that is flat for 3 weeks, drops steeply for 1 week, then is flat again for 3 weeks.
items.why: Flat parts show resting. The steep part shows a flight. A good drawing has two flat steps joined by one steep slope.

items.p: Which of these is also migration?
opts: A hilsa fish swimming from the sea up a river each monsoon to lay eggs
A crow flying from a tree to a roof
A dog walking to a gate
items.why: Migration is a regular, seasonal journey. The hilsa does it every year. A crow moving between a tree and a roof is a daily move.

items.p: Crows stay in Delhi through cold winters, and pied cuckoos migrate across the sea to India in the warm monsoon. What does this show?
opts: Migration follows food and conditions for raising young, not only cold
Cuckoos like rain more than crows
Crows cannot fly far
items.why: If cold alone caused migration, crows would leave and cuckoos would stay. Both behaviours follow food, nesting and safety.

items.p: A young migratory bird needs her parents to tell her when to leave.
items.why: False. Many birds leave at the right time with no teacher. Day length and a yearly clock inside the body help set the time. In some species, such as cranes and geese, young birds also learn the route from older birds.

items.p: The whole route that a group of migrating birds follows is called a ____.
items.why: A flyway includes the breeding grounds, the winter homes and every stopover between.

items.p: A tag should weigh no more than 5 out of every 100 parts of a bird's weight. A bar-headed goose weighs 2,000 grams. What is the heaviest tag she should carry, in grams?
items.why: 5 out of every 100 is 5 percent. 2,000 divided by 100 is 20, and 20 times 5 is 100. So the tag should weigh at most 100 grams.

items.p: In the orange-and-torch model, a dot near the top is in the dark for a whole turn when the top leans away from the torch. What does that match in real life?
opts: The far north in midwinter, with the Sun below the horizon all day
The equator at midday
The far north in midsummer
items.why: When the north leans away from the Sun, the far north gets no direct light. That is the long polar night. The same dot in the light all turn matches midsummer.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for how losing a wetland hurts a flock.
a: A wetland on the route is drained
The gap between two refuelling places gets longer
Some birds run out of fuel before the next place
The flock gets smaller over the years
items.why: The loss of a link makes a longer gap. A longer gap needs more fuel than some birds carry, so fewer arrive, and the numbers drop over the years.

items.p: A friend says: 'Birds fly south because it is cold.' Give two facts that show the idea is not complete.
items.a: Crows and sparrows stay through cold winters. Some birds, such as pied cuckoos, migrate from warm places. What matters is food and a safe place to nest.
items.why: A strong answer gives two facts that go against the claim, such as birds that stay in the cold or tropical birds that migrate, and may name food as the main reason.

items.p: Match each tool to what it tells us about migrants.
pairs: where a bird was at two points in her life
her whole route, week by week
light levels, to work out where she was after she is caught again
when a species reaches your city
items.why: Each tool shows a different part of the picture. Rings are cheap and old, tags show the route, geolocators suit small birds, radar sees flocks, and sightings come from many people.

items.p: Sort each journey as one across countries, or one within a region.
items.why: The goose, crane and falcon cross several countries. The wallcreeper and the elephant move within one region, but their journeys are still regular and seasonal.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Rosy starling, barn swallow, northern pintail, house crow.
items.a: House crow, because she lives in India all year. The other three are winter visitors.
items.why: The starling, swallow and pintail breed far to the north and spend winter in India. The house crow is a resident.

items.p: A bird waits at a stopover until the wind is behind her. Why?
opts: A tailwind carries her, so the flight costs less fuel
She likes the wind
Wind makes her feathers grow
items.why: A tailwind pushes the bird along, so she saves energy. A headwind makes the same flight cost much more fuel.

items.p: Here is a graph of a bird's position over twelve weeks. Label the three kinds of place: breeding lake, stopover and flight.
labels: A flat part at the start
A flat part in the middle
A steep part between two flat parts
items.art: A line graph with three flat steps and two steep slopes between them, over twelve weeks.
a: A flat part at the start: breeding lake
A flat part in the middle: stopover
A steep part between two flat parts: flight
items.why: Flat parts are where the bird stays, and the steep parts are where she flies.

items.p: Scientists want to put light tags on small birds to find out where they spend winter.

views.who: Nalini, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Tags show us where to protect the birds. A tag weighs only a gram.

views.who: Samir, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: Any tag changes how a bird flies. We should watch from far away.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? How could scientists check whether tags do harm?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason and suggests a fair test, such as comparing the survival of tagged and untagged birds.
items.why: Both views have a point. A fair comparison of tagged and untagged birds is how scientists check.

items.p: About two thirds of the tidal mudflats of the Yellow Sea were lost over about 50 years. What is the most likely effect on waders that refuel there?
opts: Fewer places to feed, so fewer birds survive the journey
More places to feed
No effect on birds
items.why: Waders on that flyway refuel on the mudflats. Fewer mudflats means less food and a higher chance of falling short, and counts of several waders have dropped.

items.p: Explain how a long summer day in the Arctic helps a bird raise her chicks.
items.a: The long days give plants and insects many hours of light to grow, so there is plenty of food. The bird can feed her chicks for many hours a day, even at night.
items.why: A strong answer links day length to food supply and to feeding time.

items.p: A godwit leaves with 300 grams of fat and lands with 50 grams left after 11 days. About how many grams of fat does she burn each day, rounded to the nearest gram?
items.why: 300 take away 50 is 250 grams burned. 250 divided by 11 is about 22.7, which is 23 when rounded.

items.p: A bird flies 11,000 kilometres in 8 days. How far does she fly each day on average?
items.why: 11,000 divided by 8 is 1,375. She flies about 1,375 kilometres each day, day and night.

items.p: If the Earth were not tilted, what would be different about the Arctic in June?
opts: There would be no midnight Sun, and the days would stay about 12 hours long
The Arctic would be much hotter
The Sun would never rise
items.why: The tilt makes the far north lean towards the Sun in June. Without a tilt, day length would be about 12 hours everywhere all year.

items.p: How could you test whether tags change what a bird does? Describe a fair test.
items.a: Catch two groups of the same kind of bird. Put tags on one group and leave the other alone. Follow both and compare how many survive and breed.
items.why: A strong answer has two groups that are the same except for the tag, and a measure to compare, such as survival or breeding.

items.p: A bird that stays two weeks at a stopover is wasting time.
items.why: False. The stay is when she builds the fat she needs for the next stage. Without it, she could not make the flight.

items.p: Fat holds a little more than ____ times as much energy per gram as sugar.
items.why: Fat holds about 9 units of energy per gram and sugar about 4. 9 divided by 4 is a little more than 2.

items.p: Sort each fact by the idea it supports about how a bird knows when to leave.
items: Changing the hours of light in a cage changes when birds fatten
Birds in steady light still get restless at about the right season
Shorter days in autumn bring on the urge to eat more
A caged bird in constant warmth still shows migratory restlessness
items.why: Facts about changing the light show day length at work. Facts about steady light and still getting restless show a clock inside the body.

items.p: Draw a chain from the Sun to a swallow catching an insect. Mark one place where the chain could break.
items.a: A line from the Sun to plants, to insects, to the swallow, with a mark such as a drained pond or sprayed field where the chain could break.
items.why: A strong drawing shows each link, with the energy flowing from the Sun to the swallow, and shows a break at a link that people or weather could harm.

items.p: A stopover lake in one country feeds birds from five other countries for just two weeks a year.

views.who: Anita, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The country with the lake should guard it, because it is their land and their water.

views.who: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: All five countries should help, because their birds depend on it and they gain from it.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? How could countries share the work?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side or a mix, gives a reason, and suggests a way to share, such as shared funds or shared monitoring.
items.why: Both views have a point. A flyway crosses borders, so protection often needs more than one country.

items.p: A sparrow stays in one lane all year, and a godwit flies 11,000 kilometres. Neither is wrong. Explain why both ways can work.
items.a: A sparrow can find food all year where she lives, so staying is cheap and safe. A godwit finds much more food in the far north in summer, and the gain is worth the long flight.
items.why: A strong answer says that each way works because the food and safety gained are worth the cost in each case.

items.p: In a study, tagged and untagged birds of the same kind survived equally well for three years. What does that suggest?
opts: The tags probably did little harm to survival
Tags make birds live longer
The study proves tags are never harmful
items.why: Equal survival suggests little harm, at least to survival and for that species. It does not prove that tags are harmless for all birds or in all ways.

items.p: North of the Arctic Circle, the Sun does not set for several weeks around 21 June.
items.why: True. The Earth's tilt points the far north towards the Sun at that time, so the Sun stays above the horizon all day and all night.

items.p: In a model Earth, one dot is lit for 8 of the 12 counts in one turn. What fraction of the turn is it lit, in its simplest form?
items.why: 8 out of 12 is 8 over 12. Dividing top and bottom by 4 gives 2 over 3.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Olive ridley turtle, hilsa, wallcreeper, house sparrow.
items.a: House sparrow, because she stays in the same area all year. The other three make regular seasonal journeys.
items.why: The turtle swims to nesting beaches, the hilsa swims up rivers, and the wallcreeper moves down the mountain in winter. The sparrow is a resident.

items.p: A scientist finds that a flock of waders arrives at a mudflat very thin and leaves two weeks later much heavier. What is the best conclusion?
opts: The mudflat is a refuelling stop where they build fat for the next stage
The birds have lived there all year
The birds are ill
items.why: Gaining weight in two weeks shows they are feeding well and storing fat. That is what a refuelling stop is for.

applications: Airports use radar and bird counts to warn pilots when large flocks are crossing, so planes avoid collisions.
Protecting wetlands as nature reserves and Ramsar sites, such as Chilika and Keoladeo, keeps stopovers open.
Health teams watch migrating waterbirds for diseases such as bird flu, because flocks can carry them between countries.
Planners place wind turbines and power lines away from busy flyways and narrow bottlenecks.
Citizen science projects such as eBird and Bird Count India use many people's sightings to follow migrants.
Doctors and engineers study how birds store and burn fat, and how they save energy in flight, for ideas in medicine and aircraft design.

open_questions.q: How does a young bird, who has never made the journey, know when to leave and when to stop?
open_questions.why_open: Day length and an inside clock both help. Scientists do not know how the clock works, or how it joins the light.

open_questions.q: How does a godwit sleep, or rest, during 11 days of non-stop flight?
open_questions.why_open: Some birds can rest one half of the brain at a time. Nobody has measured it for a godwit on a long flight.

open_questions.q: Why do some birds of one kind migrate and others of the same kind stay?
open_questions.why_open: In some species, part of the flock migrates and part stays. Genes, age, food and weather all seem to play a part, but nobody knows the full story.

open_questions.q: Why did the Siberian crane stop coming to Keoladeo?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists point to the loss of wetlands and to hunting along the route, but the full reasons are still debated.

open_questions.q: How will climate change affect the timing of migration?
open_questions.why_open: Some species are adjusting their dates and some are not. We do not yet know how many will keep up.

open_questions.q: Do birds feel a journey as one long trip, or as many separate days?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure what birds do. Nobody can yet say what a flight feels like to the bird.

maths.problem: In the Midnight Sun Spin, one dot was lit for 8 of the 12 counts. What fraction of the turn was it lit, in its simplest form?
maths.explain: 8 out of 12 is 8 over 12. Divide the top and bottom by 4. That gives 2 over 3. The dot was lit for two thirds of the turn.
maths.context: In the Midnight Sun Spin, you counted how long each dot on an orange stayed in the light of a torch.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you compare how much of the day each place is lit, even when the numbers of counts differ.

maths.problem: A godwit weighs 700 grams before she leaves, and about half of that is fat. How many grams of fat is that?
maths.explain: Half of 700 is 700 divided by 2. That is 350. So about 350 grams of her weight is fat.
maths.why_maths: Finding a fraction of a weight shows how big a part of the bird's body is her fuel.

maths.problem: A godwit flew about 11,000 kilometres in 8 days. About how many kilometres did she fly each day?
maths.explain: 11,000 divided by 8 is 1,375. She flew about 1,375 kilometres each day, day and night.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by the days shows how fast a journey is, so we can compare it with a car or a train.

maths.problem: A tag should weigh no more than 5 out of every 100 parts of a bird's weight. A bird weighs 300 grams. What is the heaviest tag she should carry?
maths.explain: 300 divided by 100 is 3. Then 3 times 5 is 15. So the tag should weigh at most 15 grams.
maths.why_maths: A percentage tells scientists how heavy a tag can be for birds of different sizes.

maths.problem: In the Stepping-Stone Flyway, 10 of 12 birds arrived with all four wetlands, and 6 of 12 arrived with one drained. How many more birds arrived in the first round, and what fraction of the birds fell in the second round?
maths.explain: 10 take away 6 is 4. In round 2, 12 take away 6 is 6 birds that fell. 6 out of 12 is one half.
maths.context: In the Stepping-Stone Flyway, you rolled a die to send 12 birds along a chain of wetlands twice.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two sets of counts as fractions shows how much a drained wetland changed the chance of arriving.

maths.problem: Tara the goose, an imagined bird, moved from 48 degrees north to 27 degrees north. One degree of latitude is about 111 kilometres. About how far did she travel from north to south?
maths.explain: 48 take away 27 is 21 degrees. Then 21 times 111 is 2,331. So she travelled about 2,331 kilometres from north to south.
maths.context: In the tracker graph activity, you drew a line graph of a goose's weekly latitude.
maths.why_maths: Turning degrees into kilometres lets you compare the graph with real distances.

maths.problem: A godwit flies for 11 days, rests for 2 weeks, and flies again for 5 days. How many days is that from start to finish?
maths.explain: 2 weeks is 14 days. Then 11 plus 14 is 25, and 25 plus 5 is 30. So the journey takes 30 days.
maths.why_maths: Changing weeks to days lets you add up stages of a journey that are measured in different units.

maths.problem: Suppose fat gives 9 units of energy in each gram and sugar gives 4. A bird needs 180 units for one day of flying. How many grams of fat does she need, and how many grams of sugar would she need instead?
maths.answer: 20 grams of fat, or 45 grams of sugar
maths.explain: 180 divided by 9 is 20 grams of fat. 180 divided by 4 is 45 grams of sugar. Fat is much lighter to carry, since she needs only 20 grams, not 45.
maths.why_maths: Division shows why a bird that must carry her fuel in the air prefers the fuel that holds more energy per gram.

maths.problem: Tara rested for 4 weeks at the middle stopover. She flew for 1 week before it and 1 week after it. What fraction of those 6 weeks was spent resting? Give it in its simplest form.
maths.explain: 4 weeks out of 6 is 4 over 6. Divide the top and bottom by 2. That gives 2 over 3. She spent two thirds of the time resting.
maths.context: In the tracker graph activity, you drew a goose's journey as flat and steep parts.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of a journey is rest and how much is flight, which is why stopovers matter.

roots.context: We have followed a migrating bird from the long light of the Arctic to the fat in her body and the wetlands on her way. Now we ask what that journey says about what an animal is, and where she begins and ends.

deep_truth.truth: The long days of an Arctic summer grow a flood of insects, worms and shellfish. A bird eats them and stores the energy as fat. Weeks later she burns that fat over another country. So a bird carries the sunlight of one place to another, and her body is a bridge between them.
deep_truth.habit: We say a place's wildlife is what lives inside its borders, and that a bird belongs to one country. A migrant's fuel is collected in one place and spent in another, so her body belongs to several places at once.
deep_truth.evidence: In the spinning ball, the dot near the pole stayed in the light all through a northern summer. Under that light, insects hatch, mudflat worms and shellfish thrive, and waders feed. A godwit then flies 11 days on fat alone, and the gut that held the food has shrunk.

three.who_am_i: Part of what you were made from last year came from a field, a sea or a river somewhere else. A godwit shows it more clearly: her fat comes from a marsh in one country and burns in the sky over another.
three.what_is_life: A bird in flight is burning something that grew in the sunlight of another place a few weeks ago. Life moves energy from place to place, and migrants carry it farthest.
three.what_is_this_world: The tilt of the Earth sets the length of the days, the days set the insects, the insects set the fat, and the fat sets the journey. One tilt shapes the whole yearly movement of birds.

roots.thread: Everything a godwit burns began as sunlight. Plants and algae caught it, small animals ate them, and the bird ate the small animals. The same energy then lifts her across the sea. Nothing in this chain was made by the bird. She is a place where energy passes through on its way from the Sun to the sky. Zero becomes One becomes the many, and here the many are the marsh, the midge, the godwit and the wind, all made of one flow. When you look closely, the line between the bird and her places is hard to find.

teachings.teaching: As paraphrased, the Upanishad says food is the source of all beings. From food they are born, by food they live, and into food they go back.
teachings.link: A godwit is made of the insects she ate, and she is later eaten or returns to the soil. Her body is food passing through a shape for a while.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi (Chuang Tzu), chapter 1, Free and Easy Wandering
teachings.teaching: The Chinese teacher Zhuangzi tells of a huge bird, the Peng, who rises 90,000 li on a great wind, on her way to the southern sea. A small dove and a cicada laugh at her: why go so far when a short flight to the next bush is enough?
teachings.link: A wader, a sparrow and a crow all see the same sky. The journey that looks pointless to one is the whole life of another.

science.text: Migrating birds store fat and reshape their organs before a long flight, then burn the fat in the air. We know this from weighing and measuring birds before and after.
Nobody yet knows how a young bird, who has never made the journey, knows when to leave and when to stop. A yearly clock inside her body and the length of the day both play a part.

other_view.view: Most of the energy in a marsh comes from the marsh's own plants and sunlight. A visiting flock may add or remove only a small share. They agree the link between places is real, and ask how large it is in each case. Others answer that even small flows can matter at certain times, such as the weeks before a chick hatches.

how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, people in Europe did not believe that small birds could fly to another continent. A book from 1555 even showed fishermen pulling swallows out of a frozen lake in a net, because many people thought swallows slept under the water in winter. An English writer in 1703 suggested that birds flew to the Moon. Then, in 1822, a white stork was shot near the village of Klutz in Germany with a long wooden spear stuck through her neck. The spear was not German. Experts said it came from central Africa. The stork had flown north from Africa carrying it. In 1899, a Danish teacher named Hans Mortensen began putting numbered metal rings on starlings. When a ringed bird was found far away, the ring showed where she had been. Thousands of rings now showed that birds really did cross continents, and not one was found under a lake.
how_we_found_out.who: A stork with an African spear (1822) and Hans Christian Cornelius Mortensen, a Danish teacher who began ringing birds in 1899.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people believed that swallows slept at the bottom of ponds in winter, and that small birds were too weak to cross seas. Spear-carrying storks and thousands of ring recoveries showed they fly to other continents.

quiz: Birds store fat before a long flight because fat holds more energy than anything else for its weight.
Fat is the lightest way to carry a lot of fuel, which matters when you must fly with it.
Birds migrate because it gets too cold for them.
Crows and sparrows stay through hard winters, and some tropical birds migrate; food and space matter more.
Animals migrate when what they gain from moving is bigger than the cost of the journey.
The gain is usually food, space or safety for young, and it must be worth the journey.
